q: Which measurement should be used to size table-seating allowances and row spacing in theaters and auditoriums?
n: Shoulder breadth determines the lateral space a seated person occupies, which is used to size seat widths and row-to-row allowances.

q: Provisions in a site or building intended to support a certain function or meet the specific needs of the end user, without necessarily being oriented toward comfort.
n: Facilities meet a functional need of the user even if not primarily about comfort, distinguishing them from amenities, which are explicitly comfort- or value-adding.

q: Provisions in a site or building meant to support a specific function, meet operational needs, and ease and speed up movement into, out of, and around the property for the user’s comfort.
n: Under the AFSU classification, ‘services’ are provisions — like covered driveways, ramps, and service elevators — that ease and speed up circulation, distinct from utilities (building systems) and amenities (comfort/value features).

q: Which computation produces the maximum Total Gross Floor Area (TGFAmax)?
o: AMBF x BHL in number of floors
n: TGFAmax is derived by multiplying the Allowable Maximum Building Footprint (AMBF) by the Building Height Limit (BHL) expressed as a number of floors/storeys, not by height in meters.

q: Which measurement should be factored into bunk bed design and overhead clearances above a seated position?
n: Sitting height determines the clearance needed above a seated person’s head, directly relevant to bunk beds and overhead obstructions above seating.

q: This is the regular design service phase where the architect develops initial concept drawings and preliminary line studies.
n: Schematic design is the first design phase after pre-design, translating the program into rough concept sketches and preliminary drawings prior to design development.

q: Which anthropometric measurement should guide the placement height of signage and privacy screens or partitions?
n: Eye height determines sightlines, so it governs signage placement height and the minimum height a screen or partition needs to block a line of sight.

q: Which of the following values would NOT be found listed in Table VIII.1?
n: Table VIII.1 lists the Maximum Allowable PSO, Maximum Allowable ISA, Minimum USA, and MACA by land-use zone; TOSL appears as a derived total (ISA + USA), not as a distinct ‘TOSLmax’ entry.

q: This measurement is the maximum horizontal width across the deltoid muscles.
n: Shoulder breadth (bideltoid breadth) measures the widest point across the shoulders, used for clearances like seat width and passage design.

q: This measurement is the horizontal distance from the back of the buttock to the back of the lower leg (calf).
n: Buttock-popliteal length measures seat-depth requirements used in seating design, distinct from popliteal height (knee-to-floor) or hip breadth.

q: Which measurement determines the maximum mounting height for switches, controls, levers, handles, and shelving?
n: Vertical grip reach (overhead reach while gripping) sets the practical upper limit for how high controls or shelving can be placed and still be operable.

q: Which of the following has the least direct effect on the value of PSOmax?
n: PSOmax is governed by footprint constraints — setbacks, open-space requirements, and firewalls — whereas the Building Height Limit (BHL) governs vertical massing and TGFA rather than footprint area, so it least directly affects PSOmax.

q: During this phase of the regular design service, the architect periodically supervises the ongoing construction work.
o: This is not included in the regular design service
n: The construction phase is when the architect performs general/periodic construction supervision to check the work’s conformance with the contract documents.

q: Adding the maximum allowable Percentage of Site Occupancy (PSOmax) to the maximum allowable Impervious Surface Area (ISAmax) yields which value?
n: MACA (Maximum Allowable Construction Area) is defined as PSOmax + ISAmax — the combined footprint and impervious area allowed on the lot.

q: This term describes the area at the front portion of a lot.
n: ‘Foreground’ refers specifically to the front portion of the lot, as distinguished from an easement (a legal encumbrance on part of the property) or general landscaping/entourage terms.

q: Which measurement is relevant when sizing passage clearances?
n: Maximum body breadth (the widest point of the body) sets the minimum clear width a passage needs so a person can pass through.

q: This term covers body measurements taken while at rest or while using stationary equipment like chairs, tables, and beds.
n: Static anthropometry measures the body in fixed positions (sitting, standing, at rest), unlike functional/kinetic anthropometry, which covers the body in motion.

q: This field studies how people relate to their surroundings and to the tools and equipment they use to accomplish tasks.
n: Ergonomics is the broader study of human-environment/equipment interaction, whereas anthropometry narrowly measures body dimensions.

q: This refers to a building’s electrical, electronic, mechanical, sanitary, and plumbing systems, together with their outdoor counterparts connected to the RROW or street.
n: Utilities cover a building’s systems (power, water, drainage, etc.) and their external connections to the road right-of-way, distinct from services (circulation aids) and facilities (functional features).

q: This rule for arranging a functional workspace holds that the most critical item should be placed where it is easiest to reach.
n: The importance principle prioritizes placement by how critical an item is to the task, as opposed to the frequency-of-use principle (how often it’s used) or the sequence-of-use principle (the order items are used in).

q: This term refers to government policies that regulate land use, new construction, and the extent and character of growth — essentially, the rules that steer how land gets developed.
n: ‘Development controls’ is the umbrella term for the regulatory tools (zoning, building codes, land use plans) government uses to guide how land is developed, as distinguished from any single instrument like a zoning ordinance or building code.

q: This measurement is the vertical distance from the floor to the middle of the kneecap, taken with the subject seated erect and knees at a right angle.
n: Knee height is used to determine clearance under desks and tables, measured from floor to mid-kneecap in a seated position.

q: This term refers to the scientific study of human body measurements and physical capabilities.
n: Anthropometry is specifically the measurement of the human body’s dimensions and proportions, distinct from ergonomics, which is the broader study of human-environment interaction.

q: These are provisions meant to give the user comfort or enjoyment and that raise a site’s or building’s appeal or worth.
n: Amenities are explicitly comfort/enjoyment features that add attractiveness or value, distinguishing them from facilities (functional necessity) and services (circulation/operational support).

q: This applied science focuses on designing and arranging the things people use so that user and object interact as efficiently and safely as possible.
n: This is the classic definition of ergonomics/human factors engineering — designing and arranging objects and systems for safe, efficient human use.

q: This workspace arrangement rule calls for grouping items that serve similar purposes together.
n: The function principle clusters items by shared purpose, distinct from the frequency or importance principles, which order items by use-frequency or criticality instead.

q: In the regular design service, this stage covers producing plans, elevations, sections, and outline specifications developed from the client-approved conceptual design.
n: This step follows schematic design and translates the approved concept into more detailed plans, elevations, sections, and outline specs before contract documents are prepared.

q: This measurement is the vertical distance from the floor to the crown of the head (vertex), taken while the subject stands erect looking straight ahead.
n: This is the standard anthropometric definition of ‘stature’ — standing height measured to the vertex.

q: This refers to the maximum share of a lot that a building may occupy.
n: The maximum Percentage of Site Occupancy (PSOmax) is, by definition, the Allowable Maximum Building Footprint (AMBF) expressed as a percentage of the Total Lot Area — so both terms describe the same limit.

q: This term covers measurements of a person’s capacity to perform tasks — reaching, moving through space, maneuvering — in relation to spatial and equipment design.
n: Functional anthropometry captures body capabilities during activity or motion (reach, maneuvering), unlike static anthropometry, which measures fixed dimensions.
